section.title: Rules for Priests
section.sectionRationale: Following the holiness code for the whole nation in chapters 18 through 20, attention turns specifically to the priests, who must meet a stricter standard fitting their role serving at the altar, touching mourning, marriage, and physical wholeness.
section.thesis: Because priests handle the holy food of God and represent Israel at the altar, God holds them to a stricter standard than the rest of the community regarding contact with the dead, marriage, and physical wholeness, while still including priests with defects within the priestly family and its provision.
section.frameNote: Three movements: ordinary priests and their limits on mourning contact with the dead and marriage; the high priest's even stricter standard; and priestly descendants with physical defects, who share in the priestly food but do not serve at the altar.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Speak to Aaron’s sons, the priests, and tell them that a priest is not to defile himself for a dead person among his people,
except for his immediate family, his mother, father, son, daughter, or brother,
or his unmarried sister who is near to him, since she has no husband.
He is not to defile himself for those related to him by marriage, and so profane himself.
Priests must not make bald spots on their heads, shave off the edges of their beards, or make cuts in their bodies.
They must be {{qadosh|holy}} to their God and not profane the name of their God. Because they present to the LORD the offerings made by fire, the {{lechem|food}} of their God, they must be holy.
A priest must not marry a woman defiled by prostitution or divorced by her husband, for the priest is holy to his God.
You are to regard him as holy, since he presents the food of your God. He shall be holy to you, because I the LORD am holy, I who set you apart.
If a priest’s daughter defiles herself by prostituting herself, she profanes her father; she must be burned in the fire.

units.label: The high priest, held to an even stricter standard
units.note: no loose hair, no torn garments

verses.text: The priest who is highest among his brothers, who has had the anointing oil poured on his head and has been ordained to wear the priestly garments, must not let his hair hang loose or tear his garments.
He must not go near any dead body; he must not defile himself, even for his father or mother.
He must not leave or desecrate the sanctuary of his God, for the {{nezer|consecration}} of the anointing oil of his God is on him. I am the LORD.
The woman he marries must be a virgin.
He is not to marry a widow, a divorced woman, or one defiled by prostitution. He is to marry a virgin from his own people,
so that he does not defile his offspring among his people, for I am the LORD who sanctifies him.”

units.label: Priestly descendants with a physical defect
units.note: provided for, though not serving at the altar

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Say to Aaron, ‘For the generations to come, none of your descendants who has a {{mum|physical defect}} may approach to offer the food of his God.
No man who has any defect may approach, no man who is blind, lame, disfigured, or deformed;
no man who has a broken foot or hand,
or who is a hunchback or dwarf, or who has an eye defect, a festering rash, scabs, or a crushed testicle.
No descendant of Aaron the priest who has a defect shall approach to present the offerings made by fire to the LORD. Since he has a defect, he is not to come near to offer the food of his God.
He may eat the most holy food of his God as well as the holy food,
but because he has a defect, he must not go near the veil or approach the altar, so as not to desecrate My sanctuaries. For I am the LORD who sanctifies them.’”
Moses told this to Aaron and his sons and to all the Israelites.

qadosh.gloss: Holy, set apart. Priests are called to embody this in a stricter, more visible way than the rest of Israel, since they present the food of God directly and represent the whole people before Him.

lechem.gloss: Bread or food, applied here to the offerings the priests present to God. The phrase food of their God frames sacrifice as a meal shared between God and His people, mediated through the priesthood.

nezer.gloss: Consecration, or the crown or mark of dedication, from a root meaning to separate or dedicate. Used here of the anointing oil's mark upon the high priest, and elsewhere of the golden plate on his turban and of the Nazirite's vow, all describing a life visibly set apart.

mum.gloss: A blemish, defect, or physical flaw. Used both of priests barred from altar service and of animals unfit for sacrifice elsewhere in Leviticus, the word ties visible wholeness to the symbolic requirements of approaching a holy God at the altar, without implying anything about the person's worth or standing before Him.

basic.context: This chapter sets a stricter standard for priests than for ordinary Israelites: limits on contact with the dead, restrictions on marriage, and a rule that priestly descendants with a visible physical defect may not personally serve at the altar, though they remain part of the priestly family and share in its food.
basic.hermeneutics: This is old covenant ceremonial regulation for the specific, visible office of altar service under the Mosaic priesthood. It does not describe God's view of a person's worth; the New Testament's picture of Christ deliberately including the blind, lame, and disfigured supersedes this exclusion for the church today.
basic.originalLanguages: Qadosh, holy, and lechem, the food of God, frame the priest's whole calling: he handles what is holy, so he must himself be visibly whole and set apart, nezer. Mum, blemish or defect, ties this visible wholeness to specific altar service, without touching the person's standing before God, since verse 22 explicitly says he still eats the holy food.
basic.typology: The priest barred from the altar by a physical defect, though still fed at God's table, anticipates Christ's welcome of exactly such people, the blind, lame, and disfigured, not merely to a shared meal but to full inclusion in His kingdom. The high priest's total separation from defilement by death anticipates Christ, our great High Priest, holy and undefiled, yet unafraid to touch the dead.
basic.christ: Hebrews 7:26 calls Jesus the high priest we needed: holy, innocent, undefiled, separate from sinners. Where a priest with a defect could not approach the altar, and even a healthy priest had to avoid the dead, Jesus touches the coffin at Nain and the hand of Jairus's dead daughter, and instead of becoming unclean, He gives life.
basic.god: God requires those who represent Him at the altar to embody, visibly, the wholeness fitting His holiness; yet He does not exclude priests with defects from His household or its provision, showing that exclusion from a specific function is not exclusion from belonging or care.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 7:26-28 describes Christ as the perfectly holy High Priest. Luke 7:11-15 shows Jesus touching a coffin and raising the dead without being defiled. Luke 14:13, 21 has Jesus command that the poor, crippled, lame, and blind be invited to the banquet. 1 Peter 2:5, 9 calls all believers a holy priesthood.
basic.oneStory: Israel's priesthood modeled, in visible, physical terms, the wholeness and separation holiness requires, while still caring for those it could not let serve at the altar. Christ, our perfectly whole and holy High Priest, both fulfills that pattern and reverses its exclusions, welcoming the very people it kept from the altar into the fullness of His kingdom.

context.literary:
Chapters 18 to 20 addressed 'the whole congregation of Israel,' Leviticus 19:2. Chapter 21 narrows the audience: 'Speak to Aaron's sons, the priests,' verse 1, and then narrows again to 'the priest who is highest among his brothers,' verse 10. The chapter works like a set of concentric circles drawing closer to the sanctuary. Ordinary Israelites may mourn freely; ordinary priests may mourn only for close kin, verses 1 to 4; the high priest may not defile himself even for father or mother, verses 10 to 12. The nearer a man stands to God's presence, the tighter the boundary around him.

The chapter falls into two speeches, each opened by 'the LORD said to Moses,' verses 1 and 16, and closed by a variation of the refrain 'I am the LORD who sanctifies.' That refrain runs through chapters 21 and 22 like a bell: verses 8, 15 and 23 here, and 22:9, 16 and 32. It keeps reminding the reader that the priests' holiness is God's work on them before it is their duty.

The first speech covers three areas of priestly life: death, verses 1 to 6; marriage, verses 7 and 8; and the priest's household, verse 9. The high priest's rules then repeat the same three in stricter form: death, verses 10 to 12; marriage, verses 13 to 15. The second speech, verses 16 to 23, turns from conduct to the body and lists twelve conditions that bar a descendant of Aaron from approaching the altar.

The phrase 'the food of his God' binds the chapter together, appearing in verses 6, 8, 17, 21 and 22. Priests are defined by what they handle. The chapter closes, unusually, with a note that Moses spoke these words 'to Aaron and his sons and to all the Israelites,' verse 24. The laws for priests were public knowledge; the whole nation was to know what holiness at the altar required.
context.historical:
In the ancient world death was the great defilement, and many surrounding peoples practised elaborate rites for the dead, including shaving and gashing the body. Verse 5 forbids exactly those customs, as Leviticus 19:27-28 and Deuteronomy 14:1 do for all Israel. Elijah's contest on Carmel shows the prophets of Baal who 'cut themselves with knives and lances, as was their custom,' 1 Kings 18:28. Israel's priests were to mourn differently, because they served the God of the living.

The priest's permitted mourners are listed precisely: mother, father, son, daughter, brother, and an unmarried sister 'who is near to him, since she has no husband,' verses 2 and 3. A married sister belonged to her husband's household, who would bury her. The Hebrew of verse 4 is terse, and translations differ on whether it forbids defilement for in-laws, as the BSB takes it, or refers to the priest as a husband and head of household.

The high priest was consecrated by having oil poured on his head, Leviticus 8:12, and wore the holy diadem engraved 'HOLY TO THE LORD,' Exodus 28:36. Loose hair and torn garments were the ordinary signs of grief, and also of the man with a skin disease, Leviticus 13:45. When Nadab and Abihu died, Aaron and his remaining sons were forbidden these signs and told not to leave the tent, 'for the LORD's anointing oil is on you,' Leviticus 10:6-7. Verse 12 turns that emergency ruling into a permanent law.

The list of physical defects in verses 18 to 20 reflects what any ancient reader would see at a glance. Priests served in full view of the worshippers, and the altar was a place where visible wholeness pictured the perfection of the God being approached. Ezekiel's vision of a restored temple repeats many of these rules for the priests of the future, Ezekiel 44:20-25, allowing a priest to marry 'a widow of a priest.'
context.canonical:
The priestly standard of this chapter echoes through Israel's history, mostly in its breach. Eli's sons treated the offerings with contempt, 1 Samuel 2:17, and Malachi rebukes the priests of his day: 'where is My honor?... says the LORD of Hosts to you priests who despise My name,' Malachi 1:6. He adds that 'the lips of a priest should preserve knowledge,' Malachi 2:7. Ezekiel's temple vision reaffirms the limits on mourning and marriage, Ezekiel 44:22 and 44:25, showing that the ideal outlived the failure.

The Gospels stage a vivid contrast with verse 10. At Jesus' trial, 'the high priest tore his clothes,' Matthew 26:65 and Mark 14:63, the very act this law forbade him. The man who held the office broke its outward sign while condemning the true High Priest. Jesus' parable of the good Samaritan also turns on a priest and a Levite who pass by a man left half dead, Luke 10:31-32, perhaps protecting their purity, while a Samaritan shows mercy.

Hebrews takes up the office directly. The Law 'appoints as high priests men who are weak,' Hebrews 7:28, but Jesus is 'holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners, and exalted above the heavens,' Hebrews 7:26. Every quality this chapter guarded outwardly is true of Him inwardly.

The New Testament also transfers the priestly calling to all believers. Peter calls the church 'a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ,' 1 Peter 2:5, and 'a royal priesthood,' 2:9, and Revelation says Christ 'has made us to be a kingdom, priests to His God,' Revelation 1:6. The marriage laws find their final echo in Paul's image of the church presented 'as a pure virgin to Christ,' 2 Corinthians 11:2.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to see that nearness to God raises the stakes. The whole people were holy, but the priests stood between the people and the altar, and whatever they did was done, as it were, in the doorway of God's house. The graded rules for ordinary priest and high priest taught a lesson Israel would need at every point of its history: access to God is a gift, and those who handle holy things must not treat them as common.

He also meant the people to regard their priests rightly. Verse 8 is addressed to Israel, not to the priests: 'You are to regard him as holy, since he presents the food of your God.' The nation was to honour the office, not because the man was better than others, but because of what he carried.

The rules on death carry a particular message. The priest represented the God who is life, and death was the most visible sign of the curse. By keeping away from corpses, the priest bore witness that death does not belong in God's presence.

Finally, the defect laws were meant to picture wholeness at the altar, not to rank people's worth. Moses takes pains to say that the priest with a defect 'may eat the most holy food of his God as well as the holy food,' verse 22. He stays in the family, at the table, fed by the altar he cannot serve. The first hearers would have seen that God's provision reached even those whom the symbolism of the altar required to stand back.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter prescribes rules for a particular office in a particular covenant. With the priesthood of Aaron fulfilled and superseded in Christ, Hebrews 7:11-12 and 7:18-19, the rules as rules no longer bind anyone. No Christian minister is a Levitical priest, and no believer is barred from serving Christ by a physical condition. The New Testament positively overturns that exclusion in practice: Jesus healed 'the blind and the lame' who came to Him in the temple courts, Matthew 21:14, and told His host to invite 'the crippled, the lame, and the blind,' Luke 14:13.

What carries forward is the principle that leadership among God's people calls for visible integrity. The requirement that an overseer be 'above reproach, the husband of but one wife,' 1 Timothy 3:2, applies a similar concern to the church's leaders, though it concerns character and conduct, not the body. And all believers, as priests, are called to a holiness in which the body matters, Romans 12:1, and in which grief is real but does not despair, 1 Thessalonians 4:13.

debates.question: Does the exclusion of priests with physical defects from altar service in verses 17-23 mean God devalues people with disabilities?

views.label: A symbolic requirement for a specific office, not a judgment on worth
views.case: The passage explicitly says such a priest still eats the holy and most holy food, verse 22, remaining within the priestly family and its provision. The same word for defect, mum, is used of animals unfit for the altar in Leviticus 22:20-25. On this reading the rule belongs to the visual symbolism of the sanctuary, where wholeness pictured the perfection of God, and says nothing about the man's standing before Him.

views.label: A hard text to be read honestly alongside the gospel
views.case: Others acknowledge that this text has at times been used to wound people with disabilities, and insist Christians must read it alongside the New Testament's full inclusion of people with disabilities in Christ's ministry and in the church's worship and leadership. They refuse to let the symbolism of an old covenant office outweigh the welcome of the gospel, Luke 14:21.

debates.bearing: Both views reach the same practical point. Whatever the rule's symbolic role in Israel's worship, it is not a statement about a person's worth before God, and the New Testament's picture of Christ deliberately gathering the very people this law kept from the altar governs the church today.

debates.question: Do the priestly standards of this chapter apply to Christian ministers?

views.label: Not directly, since every believer is now a priest
views.case: The New Testament never calls its elders or pastors priests in the Levitical sense. The priesthood belongs to Christ as High Priest and to the whole church as a holy priesthood, 1 Peter 2:5 and 9. Laws that set one class of Israelites apart for altar service therefore have no direct successor in church office.

views.label: By analogy, in the call for exemplary conduct
views.case: Others note that the qualifications for overseers and elders in 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:6 echo this chapter's concern that leaders' marriages and households be above reproach. The analogy is not in the rules themselves but in the principle that those who lead God's people in worship carry a heavier responsibility, James 3:1.

debates.bearing: The two views fit together. The Levitical rules are not transferred to any church office, and every believer shares in Christ's priesthood. Yet the New Testament does ask its leaders to model holiness visibly, especially in marriage and family, which is where this chapter placed its weight.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's first verb is tame, to become unclean, in its reflexive form: 'a priest is not to defile himself for a dead person,' verse 1. Verse 4 then joins it to chalal: to defile oneself is to 'profane himself.' The pair shows how the chapter thinks. Uncleanness is a state; profaning is what happens when that state is brought near what is holy. The same root chalal runs through the chapter: priests must not 'profane the name of their God,' verse 6; a priest's daughter who prostitutes herself 'profanes her father,' verse 9; the high priest must not 'desecrate the sanctuary,' verse 12, or 'defile his offspring,' verse 15; and the priest with a defect must not 'desecrate My sanctuaries,' verse 23. The BSB varies the English, but the Hebrew keeps sounding one note.

Verse 8 contains a striking use of qadash. 'You are to regard him as holy' is literally 'you shall sanctify him,' using the intensive stem. Israel does not make the priest holy in himself; they are to treat him as belonging to God. The very next clause gives the ground: 'I the LORD am holy, I who set you apart,' using the same root for what God does. Israel's honour for the priest reflects God's own act of setting apart.

The title in verse 10, 'the priest who is highest among his brothers,' is literally 'the great priest from his brothers,' hakkohen haggadol. This is where the English phrase 'high priest' comes from. The phrase 'from his brothers' matters: he is lifted from among them, not a different kind of being, which Hebrews 5:1 echoes, 'Every high priest is appointed from among men.'

The verb para in verse 10, 'let his hair hang loose,' is the same verb used for the diseased person in Leviticus 13:45 and for the forbidden mourning of Aaron's sons in 10:6. The BSB footnote offers 'must not uncover his head.' The high priest may not take the posture of the one who has been touched by death.

The nezer of verse 12, 'consecration,' comes from the root nazar, to separate or dedicate. The same noun names 'the holy diadem' fixed to the high priest's turban, Exodus 29:6, and 'the crown of consecration' on the Nazirite's head, Numbers 6:7. The Nazirite, like the high priest, was forbidden to defile himself 'even if his father or mother' died. Both were visibly set apart by what was on their heads.

Finally, mum, 'defect,' in verses 17 to 23 is the same word used for animals unfit for sacrifice, Leviticus 22:20-25, and for an injury one person inflicts on another, Leviticus 24:19. The Septuagint regularly renders it with momos, and renders the opposite quality, tamim, 'unblemished,' with amomos. That Greek word is the one the New Testament uses for Christ, who 'offered Himself unblemished to God,' Hebrews 9:14, and for the church He will present 'holy and blameless,' Ephesians 5:27. The vocabulary of the priest's body becomes the vocabulary of salvation.

typology.type: The high priest, anointed and forbidden to be defiled by death, verses 10-12
typology.fulfillment: The high priest could not go near a corpse, even of his father or mother, because the anointing oil was on him. Jesus, the Anointed One, is the High Priest who is 'holy, innocent, undefiled,' Hebrews 7:26. Yet He does what no Aaronic priest could: He touches the dead and is not defiled, because His holiness overcomes death rather than retreating from it. At Nain 'He went up and touched the coffin,' and the young man sat up, Luke 7:14-15. The type falls short because Aaron's holiness had to be protected from death; Christ's holiness defeats it, Hebrews 2:14.

typology.type: Priests barred from the altar by a defect, though still eating the holy food, verses 17-23
typology.fulfillment: The priest with a defect was fed from the altar but could not approach it. Christ reverses the boundary. He welcomes 'the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame' not only to a meal but to the banquet of the kingdom, Luke 14:21, and in the temple courts 'the blind and the lame came to Him... and He healed them,' Matthew 21:14. The escalation is that in Him people once kept at a distance are made whole and brought near, Ephesians 2:13. The final reality waits for the resurrection, when every defect is removed, 1 Corinthians 15:42-43.

typology.type: The high priest who must marry a virgin of his own people, verses 13-15
typology.fulfillment: The high priest's marriage was to be above reproach, so that his offspring would not be profaned. Paul draws on the same imagery for Christ and His people: 'I promised you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ,' 2 Corinthians 11:2. The escalation is striking. The Levitical priest had to find a bride already pure; Christ makes His bride pure, giving Himself up for her 'to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word,' Ephesians 5:25-26. Purity is His gift to her, not her qualification for Him.

typology.type: The priest who may not leave the sanctuary while the oil is on him, verse 12
typology.fulfillment: The high priest remained at his post even in grief, so that the service of God continued for the people. Hebrews presents Jesus as the High Priest who 'always lives to intercede for them,' Hebrews 7:25, having entered 'heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God,' Hebrews 9:24. The type falls short because Aaron's sons died and the office passed on, Hebrews 7:23. Christ's priesthood is permanent because He lives forever, and He never leaves the sanctuary where He intercedes.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ through the office it guards. Hebrews says, 'Such a high priest truly befits us,' and then gives a list that reads like this chapter turned inward: 'holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners, and exalted above the heavens,' Hebrews 7:26. The Levitical high priest had to be protected from defilement by rules about corpses and marriage and mourning. Jesus needed no such fence, because nothing in Him could be profaned. He is 'the Holy One of God,' Mark 1:24.

It leads to Christ by the way He handles death. The priest kept death at arm's length. Jesus walks toward it. He touches a man with leprosy, Mark 1:41, takes a dead girl by the hand, Mark 5:41, and lays His hand on the coffin at Nain, Luke 7:14. In each case the uncleanness does not pass to Him; His life passes to them. The law of contagion is reversed: holiness becomes the thing that spreads.

It leads to Christ by His own mourning. The high priest could not weep publicly over his father or mother. Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus, John 11:35, and then called him out. He is a High Priest who is 'able to sympathize with our weaknesses,' Hebrews 4:15, entering human grief without being overcome by it.

It leads to Christ by His body. The priest with a defect could not approach the veil, verse 23. Jesus, whose 'appearance was disfigured beyond that of any man,' Isaiah 52:14, was broken on the cross, and at that moment the veil was torn, Matthew 27:51. The One whose body was marred opened the way through the veil for everyone, 'through the curtain of His body,' Hebrews 10:20. The altar that excluded the maimed is replaced by a Priest who was maimed for them.

And it leads to Christ by the table. The excluded priest still ate the holy food. Christ goes further and makes all His people a priesthood, 1 Peter 2:9, who eat at His table and approach the throne of grace with confidence, Hebrews 4:16. None of this is allegory. Hebrews itself makes the link between the Levitical high priest and Christ, and the Gospels record what Jesus did with the dead and the disabled.
study.god:
This chapter shows first that God is holy in a way that orders His house. The graded rules, stricter for the high priest than for the priest, stricter for the priest than for the people, show that God's holiness is not a vague atmosphere but a presence around which everything is arranged. Nearness to Him is not casual. 'To those who come near Me I will show My holiness,' He had said when Nadab and Abihu died, Leviticus 10:3.

He is the God of the living. The priests' distance from corpses bore witness that death is an intruder in God's world, not part of His nature. Jesus would later say that He 'is not the God of the dead, but of the living,' Matthew 22:32. The rules against gashing the body and shaving the head for the dead, verse 5, also refused the pagan idea that the dead must be appeased. Israel's God needs no rites to placate the underworld.

He is the God who sanctifies. The refrain 'I am the LORD who sanctifies' in verses 8, 15 and 23 insists that holiness starts with Him. The priests were not holy by talent or pedigree but because God claimed them. That truth guards against both despair and pride: no priest could make himself holy, and none could boast of it.

He is the God who provides for those who cannot serve. The priest with a defect is fed from the altar, verse 22. His role is limited, but his place at God's table is secure. The chapter holds a real tension here: the symbolism of the sanctuary required visible wholeness, and God did not pretend otherwise, yet His care reached past the symbolism to the person. Later revelation resolves the tension from God's side. The eunuch who could not enter the assembly under Deuteronomy 23:1 is promised 'a name better than that of sons and daughters,' Isaiah 56:4-5, and an Ethiopian eunuch is baptised in Acts 8:38.

For worship, the chapter calls us to approach God with reverence, to honour those who serve Him, and to rejoice that the God who once kept the maimed from the altar has now, through a Priest wounded for us, invited everyone to draw near.

crossReferences.note: After Nadab and Abihu die, Aaron and his sons are told not to let their hair become disheveled or tear their garments, and not to leave the tent, because the anointing oil is on them. Leviticus 21:10-12 turns that emergency instruction into a permanent law for every high priest.

The Nazirite may not go near a dead body, even for father or mother, 'because the crown of consecration to his God is upon his head.' The same word, nezer, marks the high priest in Leviticus 21:12. A layperson could take on, for a season, the high priest's separation from death.

All Israel is told, 'You are sons of the LORD your God; do not cut yourselves or shave your foreheads on behalf of the dead.' Leviticus 21:5 applies the same rule to priests, grounding Israel's distinctive mourning in its relationship to the living God.

Ezekiel's vision of the future temple repeats the priestly rules on hair, marriage and contact with the dead, even listing the same family members. The ideal of Leviticus 21 is not abandoned after the exile but carried into the prophetic hope of restored worship.

At Jesus' trial 'the high priest tore his clothes,' the very act Leviticus 21:10 forbade him. The holder of the office breaks its outward sign while condemning the true High Priest, a sharp irony Matthew records without comment.

Christ is the High Priest who 'truly befits us,' holy, innocent and undefiled, unlike 'high priests men who are weak.' Every quality Leviticus 21 protected by outward rule is true of Him by nature, and He offered Himself once for all.

Jesus touches the coffin of the widow's son at Nain and raises him. Leviticus 21:1-4 kept priests from contact with the dead; Jesus, the holy High Priest, touches death without defilement because His life overcomes it.

Jesus tells His host to invite 'the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind,' and in the parable the master sends for the same people. Those who could not approach the altar under Leviticus 21:18 are the honoured guests of the kingdom banquet.

Mephibosheth, 'lame in both feet,' always ate at the king's table. His story mirrors the priest of Leviticus 21:22 who eats the holy food despite his defect, and shows the grace of a king who welcomes for another's sake.

The eunuch, excluded from the assembly by Deuteronomy 23:1, is told not to say, 'I am but a dry tree,' and is promised an everlasting name in God's house. The prophets foresee a day when bodily conditions that once barred access no longer do.

Paul presents the church 'as a pure virgin to Christ.' The marriage law for the high priest in Leviticus 21:13-14 becomes an image for Christ's relationship with His people, whom He Himself makes pure.

All believers are 'a holy priesthood' and 'a royal priesthood.' The standards once limited to Aaron's family now describe the calling of the whole church, which offers spiritual sacrifices through Jesus Christ rather than animals at an altar.

study.oneStory:
In the garden there was no need for priests. God walked with the man and woman, and death had not entered. When sin came, death came with it, and the way to God's presence was guarded by cherubim, Genesis 3:24. The priesthood of Leviticus 21 exists because of that loss. Someone must stand between a holy God and a people living under the shadow of death, and that someone must himself be kept from death's defilement.

The chapter therefore answers the fall with a picture of what restored nearness would require: a mediator set apart, unmarked by death, whole in body, above reproach in marriage. It is a picture drawn with rules, and every rule confesses that the ideal was out of reach. Priests died, and the office passed from father to son, Hebrews 7:23. Eli's sons and the priests of Malachi's day profaned what they were meant to guard.

The picture sets up the coming of a better Priest. Jesus is holy by nature, not by fence. He meets death head on and conquers it. He was marred in body so that the veil could be torn. And He does not merely feed those who were kept from the altar; He gathers them to Himself and heals them, the blind and lame in the temple courts, the outcasts at the banquet.

Through Him the priesthood widens to include all His people. They are a royal priesthood, 1 Peter 2:9, offering their bodies as living sacrifices, Romans 12:1, still called to holiness but no longer excluded by any defect of body or background.

The story ends in the new creation, where there is no more death to defile and no more mourning to restrict, Revelation 21:4. God's servants 'will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads,' Revelation 22:4, the very place the high priest once wore 'HOLY TO THE LORD.' What was once the mark of one man becomes the mark of all God's people, and His servants will worship Him, Revelation 22:3.

quiz.q: For which relatives could an ordinary priest defile himself by contact with the dead?

options.text: His immediate family: mother, father, son, daughter, brother, or unmarried sister.
options.note: Verses 1-3 list exactly this immediate family exception.

options.text: Any relative at all, without restriction.
options.note: Verses 1-4 explicitly restrict this to immediate family, excluding those related only by marriage.

options.text: No relative whatsoever; priests could never approach the dead.
options.note: Verses 2-3 explicitly permit contact for immediate family.

options.text: Only his own children.
options.note: Verses 2-3 list a broader set of immediate family members, not children alone.

quiz.q: What made the high priest's standard stricter than that of ordinary priests regarding the dead?

options.text: He could not defile himself even for his own father or mother.
options.note: Verse 11 explicitly forbids this even exception granted to ordinary priests.

options.text: He was permitted the same exceptions as ordinary priests.
options.note: Verse 11 explicitly removes the family exception ordinary priests were given.

options.text: He faced no restrictions regarding the dead at all.
options.note: Verse 11 explicitly restricts even this most basic contact for the high priest.

options.text: The text draws no distinction between the high priest and ordinary priests on this point.
options.note: Verses 10-12 explicitly draw this stricter distinction.

quiz.q: Whom was the high priest required to marry, according to verse 13?

options.text: A virgin from his own people.
options.note: Verses 13-14 specify this requirement directly.

options.text: Any widow of his choosing.
options.note: Verse 14 explicitly excludes widows from this requirement for the high priest.

options.text: No requirement is given for the high priest's marriage.
options.note: Verses 13-14 give a specific requirement.

options.text: A foreign woman from a neighboring nation.
options.note: Verse 14 specifies a virgin from his own people, not a foreigner.

quiz.q: What happened to a priestly descendant who had a physical defect, according to verses 21-22?

options.text: He could not approach the altar to offer sacrifices, but he could still eat the holy and most holy food.
options.note: Verses 21-22 state both halves of this provision explicitly.

options.text: He was completely cast out of the priestly family and its provisions.
options.note: Verse 22 explicitly states he retained his share in the priestly food.

options.text: He was required to serve at the altar despite his defect.
options.note: Verse 21 explicitly forbids altar service for such a priest.

options.text: No distinction is made regarding physical defects among priests.
options.note: Verses 17-23 make this distinction explicit and detailed.

quiz.q: How does Hebrews 7:26 describe the High Priest believers actually need?

options.text: Holy, innocent, undefiled, and separate from sinners.
options.note: Hebrews 7:26 uses this exact language of Christ.

options.text: A priest chosen by lineage from Aaron's family alone.
options.note: Hebrews explicitly argues Christ's priesthood is of a different order than Aaron's, not based on physical descent.

options.text: One who must repeatedly offer sacrifices for his own sins first.
options.note: Hebrews 7:27 explicitly contrasts Christ with priests who need to offer for their own sins first.

options.text: Hebrews gives no description of the high priest believers need.
options.note: Hebrews 7:26 gives this description directly.

questions: Priests were held to a stricter standard because of what they handled and represented before God. Where has God given you a particular role or influence that calls for a correspondingly higher level of integrity?

A priest with a physical defect could not serve at the altar, yet he still ate at God's table. Where might you be treating someone's limitation, your own or another's, as if it disqualified them from belonging, when God has not disqualified them from His provision and love?

Jesus touched the dead and the unclean and was never Himself defiled; instead, He gave life. Where do you need to bring your own uncleanness or the brokenness of someone you love directly to Him, rather than keeping a careful distance?

The high priest could not even mourn his own parents in the ordinary way, because of the weight of his calling. What costly sacrifices has following God asked of you, and how do you tend to your grief when duty and sorrow collide?
Christ welcomes the blind, lame, and disfigured not merely to a meal but to full belonging in His kingdom. Who around you needs to hear and see that kind of full welcome from you this week?

translationNotes.note: Bald spots, shaved beard edges, and cuts in the body likely refer to specific pagan mourning rites practiced among Israel's neighbors, which priests especially were forbidden to imitate.

Burned in the fire, applied to a priest's daughter who defiles herself, parallels the penalty given in Leviticus 20:14 for a distinct offense, underscoring how seriously the honor of the priestly family was regarded.

Physical defect translates mum, the same word used elsewhere in Leviticus for a blemish disqualifying an animal from sacrifice, applied here by analogy to the priest's own visible fitness for altar service, not to his standing before God.
